//: systemd OWNS FlightDeck: a unit on :80 with FLIGHTDECK_BROWSE=1, enabled at boot.
These tasks therefore drive systemctl, not flightdeck-launch.sh. The script starts a SECOND,
hand-run instance, which cannot bind :80 while the unit holds it and which systemd restarts
around anyway — so Start, Stop and Restart through it appeared to do nothing at all.
And no sudo: a polkit rule is installed for this unit, so plain systemctl works. `sudo` inside
a VS Code task waits for a password on a terminal nobody is watching, which is the other half
of why these did not work.
A change under src/ needs Restart. A change under assets/ needs only a reload — but a display
that is ALREADY OPEN keeps the script it loaded, so reload the screen as well as the browser.

tasks.label: FlightDeck: Restart
tasks.detail: After any change under src/. Assets alone only need the display reloaded.
tasks.command: systemctl restart flightdeck && sleep 3 && systemctl --no-pager --lines=0 status flightdeck && ./flightdeck-launch.sh status

tasks.label: FlightDeck: Start
tasks.command: systemctl start flightdeck && sleep 3 && systemctl --no-pager --lines=0 status flightdeck

tasks.label: FlightDeck: Stop
tasks.detail: Stops the unit. It stays enabled, so it returns when this machine restarts.
tasks.command: systemctl stop flightdeck; systemctl --no-pager --lines=0 status flightdeck || true

tasks.label: FlightDeck: Status
tasks.detail: The unit, then FlightDeck's own view: Core pairing, the Browse grant, and the addresses to reach it on.

tasks.label: FlightDeck: Enable at boot
tasks.command: systemctl enable --now flightdeck && systemctl is-enabled flightdeck

tasks.label: FlightDeck: Disable at boot
tasks.detail: Stops it and takes it out of the boot sequence — the only state in which a hand-run instance makes sense.
tasks.command: systemctl disable --now flightdeck; systemctl is-enabled flightdeck || true
